result:
The final answer q + 1 is not supported by the argument, and I believe it is wrong. I did not settle q = 3 by hand, so this rests on flaws in the proof plus a vague recollection of the literature.

**Lower bound.** The odd case (counting with maximum arc size q+1) is fine and gives k ≥ q+1. The even case also gives k ≥ q+1, but that only shows q+1 is a lower bound, not that it is attained.

**Upper bound.** This is the real gap.
- The odd case only asserts that "the fiber structure of a quadratic polynomial map" gives q arcs of size q. No construction or verification is given.
- The even case is arithmetically inconsistent. After removing the hyperoval, q² − 1 points remain. The proposal then uses q − 1 ovals of size q+1, which already cover (q−1)(q+1) = q² − 1 points. That leaves nothing for the extra (q−1)-arc it also claims.
- A partition into q+1 arcs would also have to be nearly perfect. The arcs need average size about q, close to the maximum, so almost all of them would have to be complete arcs of near-maximal size. For q odd and large, that essentially means disjoint conics. Disjoint conics are very restrictive, since q+1 of them would need (q+1)² > q²+q+1 points.

**Small cases.** The table for q = 3 and q = 4 just asserts the constructions ("three 3-arcs", "four arcs") without showing they exist. Only q = 2 is actually verified, and it is a degenerate case.

The correct value is likely larger than q+1 in general.

VERDICT: REJECT
